rule_or_criterion: (i) The descriptions of the terrain and specified distances in the historical sources imply a well defined geographical indication.
relevance_to_3Q15: Few 3Q15 names have an independent ancient locator (Achor: Eusebius; Doq: 1 Macc 16:15/Josephus; Secacah: Josh 15:61 district only).

rule_or_criterion: (ii) There exists an Arabic name which parallels the historical name in all or almost all letters and denotes a point at or reasonably near the location indicated by the historical source.

One can sometimes make the best of a somewhat inaccurate geographical reference ... provided only that the name occurs rarely in the nomenclature and is not a commonly used, standard Arabic word, which exists today in a form identical with the ancient name ... if directions and distances ... imply a clear identification, one must be content with a name that has been preserved in a faulty manner
Pottery found at the site may support an identification, but it should not be relied on in the absence of other adequate proofs ... argumentum ex silentio does not constitute proof
In a few cases epigraphic finds at or near the site have corroborated the identification
we are interested in the preservation of the name, not necessarily in the specific location of the settlement ... 'wandering of names' is not unknown
Gutturals preserved: ʿayin and ḥet generally survive in Arabic; loss of ʿayin mostly confined to the Beth-Shean–Tivʿon–Haifa strip
examples_given_by_Elitzur: ḥet preserved: Beth-Hoglah, Malḥata, Pella, Ḥammat Gader, Ḥadid, Ḥeshbon
relevance_to_3Q15: Hebrew ח should appear as Arabic ح (or خ); ه is not an attested reflex

rule_or_criterion: ḥ > ʿ rare (Transjordan-typical): ʿAmmatu–Ḥammatan > [ʿammata]; wide corpus Beth-Horon > [bēt ʿūr], Ḥammata? > [ʿamwās], Zanoaḥ > [zanūʿ]; ʿ > ḥ: ʿAzmaveth > [ḥizma]

Ancient uvular ḫ not preserved in Onomasticon survivals: Jericho ירחו > [rīḥa]; Janoah ינוח(ה) > [yānūn] (ḫ > ḥ > ø, final n added); a few ḥet > [ḫ] cases outside the corpus, possibly Arabic-root influence
Glottal h: 'not known in surviving names from the Onomasticon'; outside it Ham > [hām], one case h > ʿ
relevance_to_3Q15: No ḥet > h case cited anywhere in the gutturals section

rule_or_criterion: b preserved as b; g as ǧ (exceptions Gilgal [ǧalǧala]); d as d; k as k, with a few fricative [ḫ] cases (Michmash > [muḫmās]); p always f; t as t
Emphasis maintained consistently in Arab speech
relevance_to_3Q15: ṣ/ṭ/q should stay emphatic: penalise q↔k (e.g. ʿAkor vs ʿAqûr)

rule_or_criterion: ש generally > [s]; in Galilee and Lebanon > [š]; śin ש > [š]
Suffix -īt increases during and after the Second Temple period; list includes כוחלית
examples_given_by_Elitzur: Aεριτα, Γαβιθα, מודעית, כוחלית, Μωδιθα, Σαφιθα
relevance_to_3Q15: Talmudic כוחלית is a typical Second-Temple -īt toponym

rule_or_criterion: -at > -īt changes: עקרבת > עקרבית; עלמת (MT) > עלמית (Tg. Jon.) > [ʿalmīt]; דברת > Δαβιριθα; מרחשת–מרעשתא–ברשתה > [braʿšīt]
relevance_to_3Q15: 3Q15 כחלת vs b. Qid. 66a כוחלית fits this documented alternation (INFERENCE)
